agent_trace.summary: On abdominal CT, the small bowel, colon, mesentery, psoas muscles, abdominal wall, vertebral bodies, and major vessels are evaluated together to localize pathology and assess its extent. Abnormal bowel findings often include wall thickening, dilation, obstruction, inflammatory fat stranding, ischemia, or mass effect; mesenteric changes can help distinguish inflammatory, vascular, and obstructive processes.

key_facts: The small bowel is normally central in the abdomen and should not be markedly dilated or thick-walled.
The mesentery can show edema, stranding, or twisting when bowel pathology is present.
The colon and small bowel should be differentiated by caliber, location, and fold pattern on CT.
Abnormal abdominal pathology may also involve adjacent structures such as the psoas muscles, abdominal wall, or major vessels.
CT is well suited for identifying obstruction, inflammation, perforation, ischemia, and intra-abdominal masses.
